OT Student Urges Broader Disability Measures in Multiple Sclerosis Care
ㅤ
The Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) is the most widely used tool for measuring disability in Multiple Sclerosis, but at the Katz School’s 2025 Graduate Symposium, Arielle Caplan, a student in the Occupational Therapy Doctorate, made a compelling case that the EDSS may be missing something vital.
ㅤ
Her research explored how well EDSS correlates with patients’ actual ability to perform daily living tasks and cognitive function. She reviewed data from 160 adults with a clinical diagnosis of MS from South Shore Neurologic Associates. They categorized by EDSS disability level and then assessed on their ability to carry out Activities of Daily Living (ADL) using the Physical Self-Maintenance Scale (PSMS), as well as their cognitive performance.
ㅤ
In terms of self-care, the correlations between EDSS and PSMS scores was weak to moderate at best, and the variability in PSMS scores was greatest among the most severely disabled. This suggests that even those with high EDSS scores—typically assumed to be very disabled—may still retain surprising levels of independence.
ㅤ
In the cognitive domain, her findings echoed previous studies, showing EDSS scores to be poor indicators of cognitive decline, despite the fact that up to 70% of people with MS experience some form of cognitive impairment.
ㅤ
Dr. Gioia Ciani, director of the Occupational Therapy Doctorate program, emphasized the project’s real-world implications.
ㅤ
“Occupational therapists look at the whole person,” said Dr. Ciani. “If we’re going to support someone with MS, we need tools that reflect the actual challenges they face—not just how far they can walk. Arielle’s study is an important step toward more meaningful measurement.”
ㅤ

Meet Kira Jacoby ‘27SB, a finance major and biology minor!  

Kira has interned at Johnson & Johnson as a Strategy and Pricing Analyst Co-op, where she supported strategic pricing initiatives by building tools that helped teams make smarter, data-driven decisions. She also interned at Honor Health Network as a Corporate Finance Intern, where she gained key skills like Excel proficiency and business etiquette-but most importantly, the experience built her confidence to take on challenges and handle real responsibilities. 

She worked on projects like creating financial workups and supporting a business development plan to help the company expand into new states. The internship taught her a lot about her potential and helped her build a mindset that she can tackle anything, even when it’s unfamiliar. 

On campus, Kira served on the TAMID board as Head of Strategic Growth, leading recruitment and fundraising efforts. She also volunteers at MET Council and tutors with Solutions. 

Looking ahead, she shared, “I’m focused on finding a role that is both challenging and rewarding… It’s important to me that my work makes an impact and helps others in a meaningful way.” She plans to keep learning and pursuing opportunities that push her out of her comfort zone.  
This summer, Kira is interning at Dwight Capital as a Healthcare Intern. 

We wish her the best of luck and are incredibly proud!

Went to Leket this past week with a group of volunteers from @yeshiva_university. @leket_israel is an amazing organization that started with one man’s vision - Joseph Tzohar in 2003. The organization focuses on rescuing surplus food and redistributing it to those in need throughout Israel. Its mission is to reduce food waste and address hunger by collecting food from various sources, including restaurants, caterers, and farms, and delivering it to food banks and social service organizations. Volunteers come daily to sort and pack food. It’s a great experience.
